directions.name: The Reliability Record

positioning.category: Track record platform for student teams
positioning.statement: A place where students carry a visible record of the projects they actually finished.
positioning.differentiator: Reliability is evidenced by completed projects and teammate confirmations, not by claims in a profile.
positioning.value_proposition: Pick teammates on evidence instead of hope.

directions.audience_focus: Students who have already been burned by a teammate dropping out
directions.tagline_direction: Proof over promises: language about what someone has finished, not who they say they are
strengths: Turns the vague fear of an unreliable teammate into something checkable
Gets stronger the longer a student uses it
risks: First-year students with no record look unhireable
A reliability score can feel like surveillance
directions.why_this_lens: The sharpest wedge here is evidence of follow-through, which no group chat can offer.
obvious_ideas_rejected: A five-star rating system for teammates — every marketplace bolts ratings onto profiles, and students would game it within one term.
LinkedIn for students — the obvious category grab, which means competing with LinkedIn on its own ground.
A skills-matching algorithm — the default answer for any "find people" product, and it says nothing about whether someone shows up.

directions.name: Crew Call

positioning.statement: Post the project you want to make and let the right crew answer the call.
positioning.differentiator: The project comes first and people apply to it, instead of people browsing each other.
positioning.value_proposition: Describe the thing you want to build and assemble a crew around it.

directions.audience_focus: Ambitious students with an idea and no team yet
directions.tagline_direction: Film-set language: calls, crews, credits and premieres
strengths: Gives the product an identity nothing else on campus has
Makes starting a project feel like an event rather than admin
risks: The metaphor may read as creative-only and put engineers off
Needs enough projects posted to feel alive
directions.why_this_lens: A distinctive world makes students want to be seen using it, which is how campus products spread.
obvious_ideas_rejected: A campus social network with a projects tab — the safe framing every student app starts from, and it dies without daily use.
Swipe-to-match for teammates — the reflex metaphor for pairing people, and it makes a real commitment feel disposable.
Friendly pastel study-buddy branding — the visual default for student tools, so it looks like every app already on their phone.

directions.name: Nobody Ghosts

positioning.category: Commitment layer for student group work
positioning.statement: Teams agree what each person owes the group before the work starts, and the app holds them to it.
positioning.differentiator: It solves what happens after the team forms, which is where students actually get hurt.
positioning.value_proposition: Agree who does what up front, so nobody carries the whole project alone.

directions.audience_focus: Students stuck in assigned coursework groups they did not choose
directions.tagline_direction: Plain, reassuring language about fairness and carrying your share
strengths: Speaks to the pain the founder actually described
Works even for groups students did not choose
risks: Sounds like an admin tool rather than something students want
Harder to make appealing before a bad experience happens
directions.why_this_lens: Students do not want a network; they want not to be let down again.
obvious_ideas_rejected: A group-chat replacement — the predictable "students already use WhatsApp" answer, which fights a habit instead of a problem.
A productivity tracker for group projects — the obvious management framing, which students experience as surveillance.
An "empowering collaboration" platform — the phrase every student tool uses, and it promises nothing anyone can check.

directions.name: Finish Rate

positioning.statement: The only student profile that shows how often you finish what you start.
positioning.differentiator: One honest number, earned over time, that no CV line can fake.
positioning.value_proposition: Show you finish, and the good teams come to you.

directions.audience_focus: Students who deliver and want it to be visible
directions.tagline_direction: Scoreboard language, owned by the student rather than imposed on them
strengths: Rewards the students you most want on the platform
risks: Punishing for anyone who had one bad semester
directions.why_this_lens: A single legible signal is the fastest way into a crowded campus market.
obvious_ideas_rejected: A verified-skills badge system — the standard credential play, and badges say what you can do, not whether you finish.
A leaderboard of top students — the obvious gamification move, which rewards the already-visible and discourages everyone else.
A recruiter-facing talent pool — the predictable monetisation framing, which changes who the product is really for.

directions.name: Build Night

positioning.statement: The place where student projects get started on a Tuesday night and finished by the weekend.
positioning.differentiator: Built around short, time-boxed builds rather than open-ended team hunting.
positioning.value_proposition: Find people who want to build the same thing this week.

directions.audience_focus: Hackathon-minded students who work in bursts
directions.tagline_direction: Late-night making, pizza, deadlines and shipping
strengths: Creates repeatable moments to market around
risks: Depends on local density of active students
directions.why_this_lens: Culture, not features, is what makes students bring their friends.
obvious_ideas_rejected: A hackathon listings board — the obvious utility framing, and listings are a commodity nobody feels loyal to.
"Build your dream team" language — the phrase every team-formation tool opens with, and it promises an outcome the product cannot guarantee.
A Discord server with structure — the default community answer, which inherits Discord's noise problem.

directions.name: Fair Share

positioning.statement: Every group project starts with a shared agreement about who carries what.
positioning.differentiator: Designed for the assigned group nobody chose, which is where most of the pain sits.
positioning.value_proposition: Make the split explicit before resentment sets in.

directions.tagline_direction: Language about fairness, clarity and carrying your share
strengths: Useful from the first minute, with no network needed
risks: Little reason to open it between projects
directions.why_this_lens: The audience's real fear is being left carrying the work, not being unable to find people.
obvious_ideas_rejected: A peer-review score after each project — the obvious accountability mechanism, which turns classmates into assessors.
A contract template generator — the predictable "make it formal" answer, and students will not sign paperwork with friends.
A workload-splitting calculator — the obvious fairness tool, which measures effort instead of building trust.
